hook.speaker: Bharata
hook.setting: Grieving Kausalya accuses Bharata of plotting Ram's exile; he knew nothing of it.
hook.sanskrit: आर्ये कस्मादजानन्तं गर्हसे मामकल्मषम्। विपुलां च मम प्रीतिं स्थितां जानासि राघवे॥
hook.line: Why blame me, who knew nothing? You know what I feel for him.
hook.translation: Noble lady, why do you blame me, who knew nothing and did nothing wrong? You know how deep my love for Ram is.
hook.why: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

prasang.title: Bharata wrongly blamed
prasang.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.
prasang.story_hook: He had done nothing, and the one person whose good opinion he needed was sure he had done it all.
prasang.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

hook.for_you: You feel small when guests watch, and this verse says you knew nothing and did nothing wrong.

alternates.speaker: Bhartrihari
alternates.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
alternates.sanskrit: खलालापाः सोढाः कथमपि तदाराधनपरैः निगृह्यान्तर्बाष्पं हसितमपि शून्येन मनसा । कृतो वित्तस्तम्भप्रतिहतधियामञ्जलिरपि त्वमाशे मोघाशे किमपरमतो नर्तयसि माम् ॥
alternates.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
alternates.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?
alternates.why: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

alternates.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
alternates.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
alternates.sanskrit: अरणीमग्निकामो वा मथ्नाति दहृयं मम / वाचा दुरुक्तं देवर्षे तन्मां दहति नित्यदा
alternates.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
alternates.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.
alternates.why: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

prasang.title: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasang.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
prasang.story_hook: Krishna, who guided a war, admitted to a sage that he could not keep the peace in his own family.
prasang.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Letter from the USA, 9 July 1895, on opposition to his work in America.
verse.line: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance.
verse.translation: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Each man who thinks ahead of his time is sure to be misunderstood.
verse.why: Ridicule and opposition are stages, not verdicts.

prasang.title: Ridicule, opposition, acceptance (letter to Khetri, 1895)
prasang.summary: Facing opposition from some clergy in America, he writes to his friend the Maharaja that every work passes through ridicule, opposition and then acceptance. Anyone ahead of their time will be misunderstood, so he will stay steady.
prasang.lesson: Ridicule and opposition are stages, not verdicts.

verse.try_today: Notice one small act of your own work today and let it stand for itself.

why: being mocked and opposed for one's work

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse.sanskrit: स नैव व्यभवत् तच्छ्रेयो रूपमत्यसृजत धर्मम् । तदेतत्क्षत्रस्य क्षत्रं यद्धर्मस्तस्माद्धर्मात् परं नास्त्यथो अबलीयान् बलीयाꣳसमाशꣳसते धर्मेण यथा राज्ञैवम् । यो वै स धर्मः सत्यं वै तत् तस्मात्सत्यं वदन्तमाहुर्धर्मं वदतीति धर्मं वा वदन्तꣳ सत्यं वदतीत्येतद्ध्येवैतदुभयं भवति ॥
verse.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.
verse.why: Fear and loneliness are human; truth gives even the weak a footing.

prasang.title: The first being: fear, loneliness and dharma
prasang.summary: In this creation story the first being, alone, feels fear, then realises there is no one else to fear. He feels no joy alone and longs for a companion, splitting into husband and wife. Finally dharma is created, the truth by which even the weak can stand up to the strong.
prasang.lesson: Fear and loneliness are human; truth gives even the weak a footing.

verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you speak your truth, and let it stand.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the room, and dharma stands with you.

why: With what is right the weak can face the strong.
the wronged person is told their ground is the highest there is

verse.speaker: Bhishma
verse.setting: Bhishma on public slander, answering Yudhishthira's question about being insulted in an assembly.
verse.sanskrit: परिवादं ब्रुवाणो हि दुरात्मा वै महाजने / प्रकाशयति दोषान्स्वान्सर्पः फणमिवोन्नतम्
verse.line: Whoever runs others down in public only puts their own faults on display.
verse.translation: The person who speaks ill of others in front of a crowd only puts his own faults on display, the way a snake raises its hood.
verse.why: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.

prasang.title: Bhishma on bearing slander
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to respond when a harsh fool abuses you in public. Bhishma: let it pass like a crow cawing; the slanderer only displays his own faults.
prasang.lesson: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.

verse.try_today: Notice what is on display when someone speaks ill of you in public.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the room while a snake raises its hood and shows its own face.

why: The public insult is turned back on the one who made it
The slandered person is not the one exposed

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.line: The remedy for weakness is not brooding over weakness, but thinking of strength.
verse.translation: But, says the Vedanta, being reminded of weakness does not help much; give strength, and strength does not come by thinking of weakness all the time. The remedy for weakness is not brooding over weakness, but thinking of strength.
verse.why: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

prasang.title: Practical Vedanta 1: faith in yourself (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Vedanta must work in ordinary life. Calm minds do the most work, angry ones break themselves. The new religion calls the person who does not believe in himself the atheist, and the remedy for weakness is to think of strength, not brood over weakness.
prasang.lesson: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

verse.for_you: You carry the weight of a home and an office, and someone is making you feel smaller. That silence around you is not your failure. The remedy is to think of the strength it takes to show up every day.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing you did well today that required real strength.
verse.scene_line: Beside the guests, the silence of the one you live with holds no power over the quiet strength you carry.

why: Think of strength, not of weakness.
turn the mind to what is strong in you

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: The poet to the chataka, a bird said to drink only raindrops from clouds.
verse.sanskrit: रे रे चातक सावधानमनसा मित्र क्षणं श्रूयताम् अम्भोदा बहवो वसन्ति गगने सर्वेऽपि नैकादृशाः । केचिद्वृष्टिभिरार्द्रयन्ति धरणीं गर्जन्ति केचिद्वृथा यं यं पश्यसि तस्य तस्य पुरतो मा ब्रूहि दीनं वचः ॥
verse.line: Some clouds bring rain, some only thunder. Don't plead with everyone you meet.
verse.translation: Friend chataka, listen carefully for a moment. Many clouds live in the sky, but not all are alike. Some drench the earth with rain; some only thunder for nothing. Do not speak pleading words before every cloud you see.
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

verse.try_today: Notice who offers help and who only makes noise.
verse.scene_line: You stand in a room full of thunder, asking for rain.

why: Keep one's asking for those who can and will help
Tell the giver from the thunderer

story.title: A boy bent in eight places walks into the king's court, and the court laughs
story.story_hook: He was twelve, bent in eight places, and the court laughed when he walked in. He laughed back, and then he won.
story.summary: Ashtavakra was born with his body bent in eight places. As a boy of about twelve he learns that his father lost a debate at King Janaka's court to the scholar Bandi and was made to pay with his life. He walks to the palace. The gatekeeper will not let a child in.
story.lesson: A person is to be measured by what they know and are, not by age or body.
story.teaser: He was twelve, bent in eight places, and the court laughed when he walked in. He laughed back, and then he won.
story.for_you: Your body is not the measure of what you know. The silence in your home is not the verdict on your worth. You carry the full weight of your day and your mind. Let that be enough.

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse.sanskrit: अवलेपः समुद्रस्य न दर्शयति यः स्वयम्। प्रशमश्च क्षमा चैव आर्जवं प्रियवादिता॥ असामर्थ्यफला ह्येते निर्गुणेषु सतां गुणाः।
verse.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.
verse.why: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.
verse.misuse: Firmness only after real patience, and only toward someone who keeps ignoring you. When the ocean finally came, Ram listened and redirected the arrow.

prasang.title: Ram at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasang.summary: Ram lies on kusha grass by the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way. Ignored, he tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness and takes up his bow. The ocean rises, offers a way (Nala's bridge), and Ram releases the arrow elsewhere at its request.
prasang.story_hook: For three days the prince lay on a bed of grass at the edge of the sea, asking politely.
prasang.lesson: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.

why: patience was offered and treated as incapacity
Humble first, firm after (Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 21-22)

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: न त्वेवात्माऽवमन्तव्यः पुरुषेण कदाचन / न ह्यात्मपरिभूतस् भूतिर्भवति शोभना
verse.line: Never look down on yourself. Nothing good grows from self-contempt.
verse.translation: A person should never look down on himself. The one who despises himself never finds real prosperity.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

why: Think of strength, not of weakness.
Forbids self-contempt outright

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse.sanskrit: न श्रेयः सततं तेजो न नित्यं श्रेयसी क्षमा / इति तात विजानीहि द्वयमेतदसंशयम्
verse.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.
verse.why: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.misuse: Forgiveness never means accepting ongoing harm; this verse itself says it has limits.

prasang.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.story_hook: Thirteen years into exile, Draupadi looked at her husband and asked why he was not angry.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you choose your own steadiness over their noise.

why: With what is right the weak can face the strong.
Know the time for firmness and the time for forbearance; ask first, then stand.

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
verse.line: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
verse.translation: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
verse.why: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

prasang.title: Learn from all, imitate none (Lahore, 1897)
prasang.summary: Speaking to rival reform and orthodox groups, he looks for common ground. Religion must be realised, not repeated like a parrot. Learn everything good from others, as a seed takes in earth, air and water, but grow into your own tree and do not become others.
prasang.lesson: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

verse.for_you: You have a full day and a home to run. You can take what is good from this life and leave the rest. You do not have to become a copy of the people around you.
verse.try_today: Notice one small act of kindness from someone today and let it land in your own way.

why: stay yourself while learning
take what is good, leave the rest

verse.speaker: Shiva
verse.setting: Shiva, when Sati wants to attend her father's ceremony uninvited, where Shiva is resented.
verse.sanskrit: जदपि मित्र प्रभु पितु गुर गेहा। जाइअ बिनु बोलेहुँ न सँदेहा॥ तदपि बिरोध मान जहँ कोई। तहाँ गएँ कल्यानु न होई ॥
verse.line: You may visit family without an invitation. But where there is hostility toward you, going brings no good.
verse.translation: It is true that one may go uninvited to the home of a friend, a master, a father or a teacher. Yet where someone holds hostility toward you, no good comes of going there.
verse.why: You may go to family without an invitation, but not into open hostility; listen to that warning.
verse.misuse: Not a rule to cut off family; a caution about walking into known hostility.

prasang.title: Sati goes to her father's sacrifice uninvited
prasang.summary: Sati's father Daksha holds a great sacrifice and invites everyone except Shiva and her. Shiva warns her that going where there is hostility brings no good, but she goes. Her father ignores her and insults her husband in front of everyone, and the visit ends in catastrophe.
prasang.story_hook: The sky over Kailash filled with chariots heading to her father's feast, and none of them had come for her.
prasang.lesson: You may go to family without an invitation, but not into open hostility; listen to that warning.

verse.for_you: You leave the office and enter a room where you are belittled. There is no good that comes of staying in that hostility.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you choose to step back from a room that holds contempt.
verse.scene_line: You stand beside Sati, who is about to enter a home where her husband is held in contempt.

why: self-respect may decline a room that holds contempt
custom allows the visit, judgement looks at the host's heart

queries.diagnose: Hurt grows from expecting others to act as we want; no one else can give us sorrow unless we hand them the reins of our peace.
queries.steady: Each person acts from their own nature; what they do is theirs to carry, and how you respond is yours.
queries.act: Do your own duty toward them with patience and respect, accept what is theirs to choose, and keep your peace in your own hands.

plan_v3.first_line: You feel small when guests watch, and this verse says you knew nothing and did nothing wrong.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse.sanskrit: खलालापाः सोढाः कथमपि तदाराधनपरैः निगृह्यान्तर्बाष्पं हसितमपि शून्येन मनसा । कृतो वित्तस्तम्भप्रतिहतधियामञ्जलिरपि त्वमाशे मोघाशे किमपरमतो नर्तयसि माम् ॥
verse.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?
verse.why: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

verse.for_you: You fold your hands after your office job and still prepare the home for guests who belittle you. You do not need to keep dancing for their approval. The work you do is enough.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you refuse to laugh at a belittling comment.

why: Swallowed insults
Folding hands before people numbed by money

verse.speaker: Vibhishana
verse.setting: Insulted for urging Ravana to return Sita, Vibhishana leaves the court with these words.
verse.sanskrit: सुलभाः पुरुषा राजन्सततं प्रियवादिनः। अप्रियस्य च पथ्यस्य वक्ता श्रोता च दुर्लभः॥
verse.line: Flatterers are easy to find. Rare is the one who tells the hard truth, rarer the one who hears it.
verse.translation: O king, people who always say pleasant things are easy to find. Someone who says what is unwelcome but good for you is rare, and so is someone who will listen to it.
verse.why: Speak the truth to family even when it costs you; leave if you must, without hatred.

prasang.title: Vibhishana tells his brother the truth
prasang.summary: In Ravana's war council, everyone else flatters him. Vibhishana alone says what he has seen: return Sita, avoid war. Ravana insults him as a traitor. Vibhishana says flatterers are easy to find and truth-tellers rare, wishes his brother well, and leaves.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone in the hall agreed with the king, except his youngest brother.
prasang.lesson: Speak the truth to family even when it costs you; leave if you must, without hatred.

verse.for_you: You carry the weight of work and the sting of public belittlement. The one who stays silent in the room is the one who makes the truth feel rare.
verse.try_today: Notice one person today who speaks a hard truth without flattery, and simply hear it.
verse.scene_line: You stand among flatterers while the one who speaks the hard truth is cast out.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: कदर्थितस्यापि हि धैर्यवृत्तेर्न शक्यते धैर्यगुणः प्रमार्ष्टुम् । अधोमुखस्यापि कृतस्य वह्नेर्नाधः शिखा याति कदाचिदेव ॥
verse.line: Turn a torch upside down and its flame still rises. Steadiness survives humiliation.
verse.translation: Even when harassed, the steadfast cannot be robbed of their steadiness. Hold a torch upside down: its flame never points downward.
verse.why: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

verse.for_you: You have done your work and you have done it well. The flame inside you is not theirs to turn downward. Let it keep its own direction.
verse.try_today: Notice the flame that still points upward in you today.
verse.scene_line: The torch of your steadiness burns upward even while they belittle you in front of guests.

why: One's nature is not in the hands of those who mistreat one
Humiliation does not reach what one is

verse.speaker: Bhishma
verse.setting: Yudhishthira asks how a calm person should respond when a loud fool insults him in public.
verse.sanskrit: प्रकृत्या हि प्रशंसन्वा निन्दन्वा किं करिष्यति / वने काक इवाबुद्धिर्वाश्यमानो निरर्थकम्
verse.line: Whether a careless person praises or blames you, what can it do? It's a crow cawing in the forest.
verse.translation: Whether such a person praises you or blames you, what difference can it make? It is like a senseless crow cawing in the forest, meaning nothing.
verse.why: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.
verse.misuse: Fair criticism is worth hearing; this is about mindless abuse.

prasang.title: Bhishma on bearing slander
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to respond when a harsh fool abuses you in public. Bhishma: let it pass like a crow cawing; the slanderer only displays his own faults.
prasang.lesson: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.

verse.for_you: Their words are empty noise. You carry the weight of your own dignity, not theirs. Keep your footing today.
verse.try_today: Notice their words as a sound without meaning.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your home, and their voices become a crow cawing in the forest.

why: The abuse is reduced to noise
Mindless blame is given no weight

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Victoria Hall, Madras, February 1897.
verse.line: anything that makes you weak physically, intellectually, and spiritually, reject as poison;
verse.translation: And here is the test of truth — anything that makes you weak physically, intellectually, and spiritually, reject as poison; there is no life in it, it cannot be true. Truth is strengthening.
verse.why: Judge ideas, and habits, by whether they make you stronger.

prasang.title: 'Reject it as poison' (Madras, 1897)
prasang.summary: He answers critics who claimed others made his American success, noting how quickly sympathy vanishes when you dare to differ. His test of truth: whatever makes you weak in body, mind or spirit, reject as poison.
prasang.lesson: Judge ideas, and habits, by whether they make you stronger.

verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you stand up straighter and let that be enough.

why: choose what strengthens
the strength test for truth

verse.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Brihaspati counsels Indra on how to hold authority among difficult people.
verse.sanskrit: मृदुमप्यवमन्यन्ते तीक्ष्णादुद्विजते जनः / मातीक्ष्णो मा मृदुर्भूस्त्वं तीक्ष्णो भव मृदुर्भव
verse.line: People walk over the soft and fear the harsh. Be firm when it's needed, gentle when it's needed.
verse.translation: People look down even on the gentle, and they shrink from the harsh. Do not be only harsh, do not be only soft: be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
verse.misuse: Firmness here means clarity, not cruelty.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you can be firm and clear in your voice.

why: Firmness is given a rightful place
Knowing which the moment needs

story.title: Karna is asked for his lineage and has no answer
story.story_hook: He had just equalled the best archer in the world. Then someone asked: and who is your father?
story.summary: Karna walks into the royal arena uninvited and matches every feat Arjuna has just performed. He challenges him to single combat. Then Kripa asks him to announce his mother, father and royal house, because princes do not duel men of unknown family. Karna's face falls like a lotus beaten down by rain.
story.lesson: A person shut out for his birth will give everything to the one who first treats him as an equal.
story.teaser: He had just equalled the best archer in the world. Then someone asked: and who is your father?
